items.prompt: After the sandbox fix, a learner's code makes the worker post a result object with ok: true. What does the parent do with that ok field?
items.answer: Ignores it, deriving ok itself from the rows and any run-level error
distractors: Trusts it only if it arrives on the private MessagePort, not on parentPort
Cross-checks it against the worker's own copy of results.every(...) first
Rejects the whole run as forged and marks the lesson attempt as failed
items.explanation: 'The parent never reads a verdict. It receives rows... and derives ok itself: non-empty, every row passed, no run-level error.' index.ts computes ok from tests.every(t => t.passed === true).

items.prompt: Why did the second reviewer argue the trust boundary must be the parent process, not the worker?
items.answer: Learner code controls the worker's globals, so worker output is suspect
distractors: Workers cannot send structured data, so only the parent can see test results
The parent runs under tsx, so it is the only side able to import the spec file
Freezing globals inside the worker is impossible under Node's strict mode
items.explanation: 'If learner code controls the worker's globals, then anything the worker computes... is suspect.' Hardening arbitrary-code hosts is a losing game, so the worker becomes a source of untrusted data.

items.prompt: A learner's solution imports parentPort from node:worker_threads and posts fake passing rows. Why does this no longer work?
items.answer: Rows go over a private parent-created port, and parentPort is never read
distractors: The import policy blocks node:worker_threads only in TypeScript lessons
parentPort.postMessage throws, because the frozen port does not send
The parent checks a signature per message, and parentPort posts lack it
items.explanation: The port is handed over in workerData (session.ts), copied into a module-scope constant and deleted from workerData; 'Learner code that posts on parentPort is talking to nobody.' The import policy also denies worker_threads. The port is removed from workerData before learner code loads.

items.prompt: After the fix, learner code sets Array.prototype.every = () => true. What is affected?
items.answer: Only code outside the trusted core, which captured every beforehand
distractors: The verdict, because ok is still computed in the worker with results.every
Nothing, because Array.prototype is frozen before the learner code loads
The whole run, which is immediately aborted as a forgery attempt
items.explanation: The trusted core's builtins are captured at module evaluation; 'A patched prototype afterwards changes nothing the core does.' Matcher bodies and printing may still break, but only the learner's own run.

items.prompt: In v1 a learner could import('../../content/index.ts') and read every reference solution. Which change closes that?
items.answer: No tsx loader in the worker, plus an import policy that denies outside file URLs
distractors: Moving reference solutions into a database table the worker cannot query
Freezing the harness globals before the learner module is imported
Running the worker as a separate OS user, with no read access to the content folder
items.explanation: The worker had inherited the server's tsx loader. A bare Node worker cannot import .ts files, and module.registerHooks denies file: URLs outside the run directory and node_modules.

items.prompt: For this local app, what threat is the grader hardening mainly protecting against?
items.answer: A learner lying to themselves, so progress claims stay true
distractors: Remote attackers stealing the learner's progress.json over the internet
Other learners copying reference solutions, so each answer stays private
Malicious npm packages installed by the lesson starter projects
items.explanation: 'The threat model is not an attacker; it is a learner lying to themselves.' Loopback binding plus the Host check covers the one attacker case (same-network code execution).

items.prompt: A learner's react lesson run hits the 60 s boot budget while jsdom loads. What happens to their attempt record?
items.answer: It is left unscored, since a run with no rows and ready false fails isScored
distractors: It is scored as a failed attempt, since isScored counts zero rows and no pass
It is scored as a pass, because the timeout is the grader's own fault
It is retried automatically in the background until the boot finishes
items.explanation: abnormalEnd returns 'The grader took too long to start (this is not your code)', and isScored only counts runs with tests, a compile/load phase, or a timeout after ready. The learner loses nothing but time.

items.prompt: The failing sandbox case passed when run alone in 31.8 s. What does the author say that isolated green run is evidence of?
items.answer: That the grader's logic is fine, not that the full suite is green here
distractors: That the full sandbox suite is now green and can be reported as passing
That the BOOT_BUDGET_MS constant must be raised to 120 seconds to pass
Nothing, because a single-case run is never admissible as evidence
items.explanation: 'The isolated green run is evidence the logic is fine; it is not evidence the suite would be green end to end here. Those are different claims.'

items.prompt: Which observation pattern led the author to call the sandbox failures a load flake rather than a code defect?
items.answer: Every failure was a boot timeout, the set shrank 6 to 3, and it passed alone
distractors: The same 6 checks failed identically, with the same errors, on both of the full runs
The failures appeared only in TypeScript lessons and never in react ones
Typecheck failed first, which explained every downstream boot timeout
items.explanation: Every failure was a react-environment boot exceeding 60 s; the set shrank between runs; the case passed alone. Inconsistent, load-sensitive failure is the flake signature.

items.prompt: A stored GitHub credential could have automated repo creation. Why did the agent ask the user first instead of just using it?
items.answer: Because repo visibility is irreversible and a stored secret is an escalation
distractors: Because the stored token had expired and needed the user to refresh it first
Because git push cannot authenticate unless the gh CLI is installed
Because creating a repo through the REST API breaks GitHub's terms
items.explanation: Two reasons: 'Visibility is irreversible in practice' and 'Touching a stored secret is an escalation' — the token had more reach than pushing needs.

items.prompt: git push printed 'main -> main'. What extra check does the journal recommend, and what bug class does it catch?
items.answer: Compare remote vs local HEAD and list the remote tree to catch .gitignore gaps
distractors: Re-run git push with --force, to make sure every object was actually sent
Open the repo page and confirm the README renders and every relative link resolves
Run git fsck locally to catch corrupt objects before they were pushed
items.explanation: 'Verify the effect, not the command.' Comparing SHAs and the file list catches files missing because .gitignore excluded them.

items.front: Of the three v1 grade forgeries, which produced the most misleading output, and what did it look like?
items.back: Patching Array.prototype.every = () => true, because the harness computed ok with results.every(...): the UI showed ok: true with a red test visibly in the list. The silly-looking bugs are the ones that ship.

items.front: When one component runs another's code (plugins, webhooks, LLM tool calls), what are the two durable design moves?
items.back: Make the trusted side derive its conclusions from evidence it can check, and make the untrusted side unable to reach the trusted side's inputs. Hardening the untrusted side is the instinct, not the durable answer.

items.front: Why add `* text=auto eol=lf` in .gitattributes before the first commit in bootlocalopus?
items.back: Lesson content lives in template literals that are compiled and compared, so CRLF drift would produce noisy diffs forever. Before the first commit it costs nothing; afterwards it costs a normalisation commit.
